newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate to start tax cut debate Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate to start tax cut debate Wednesday.

text.p: Senate leaders scheduled debate on tax legislation to begin Wednesday, one day before the House where a companion bill was undergoing late adjustments.
With 20 hours of debate set aside for its five-year tax cut plan, the Senate was unlikely to vote on it until the end of the week, parliamentarians said.
Because of changes in the Senate Finance Committee last week, the Senate bill contained an actual net tax cut of $77 billion, with provision for $8 billion in child health spending.

A budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said any final bill hammered out with the House must include the full $85 billion net tax reduction.
"I will not be happy with any final product that does not have a net $85 billion," the Mississippi Republican said.
The House of Representatives was expected to debate and vote on its tax bill Thursday, because few amendments were likely to be allowed on the floor.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer proposed to the Rules Committee that two hours of total debate be allowed on the floor for the tax bill and a very limited number of amendments be permitted to be offered.
The Texan also proposed some changes to the House Republican bill. Those included leaving an ethanol subsidy intact through its expiration at the end of 2000 and then eliminating it after that.
The original proposal would have gradually reduced the subsidy through 2000, and Archer said he made the change to accommodate lawmakers who protested the subsidy reduction.
"My major goal is to be sure that people get the message not to build new facilities in anticipation that this credit will be extended after the year 2000. It will not be extended," Archer said.
Another change would enable married taxpayers who receive dependent care credit also to get child tax credit if their income is below $60,000.

Archer also proposed a change to the bill aimed at ensuring deficits did not worsen in 1999. That provision would allow airline ticket taxes required to be deposited from July 1, 1998, through September 30, 1998, to be deposited on Oct. 13, 1998. That way the money received by the government would register in the fiscal year that starts Oct. 1.

Archer further proposed directing the secretary of the Treasury to conduct a study of whether a repeal of the depreciation adjustment for minimum tax purposes would result in allowing any companies to pay no federal income tax.
White House officials met with House Democrats to discuss spending and tax legislation Tuesday.

Lawmakers who were in that meeting said there was strong White House and House Democrat opposition to the House Republican tax bill. When the bill was considered in the House Ways and Means Committee, all the Democrats voted against it.
White House officials at the meeting were "vehemently opposed" to the House Republican tax bill, Rep. John LaFalce, a New York Democrat, said.
